paragraphs: This paper describes a convolutional neural network system that follows a hand through video and recognizes whether it is open or closed. These are two related tasks: locating the hand establishes where to look, while gesture recognition determines its state. The system is intended to work across users, making variation between people part of the recognition problem.

The reported test set contains video sequences from 18 individuals recorded in 18 room environments. In 99.7% of test frames, the tracked position falls within 10 pixels of the correct location. The gesture network identifies the open or closed state correctly in 99.1% of frames. These figures measure different aspects of performance and should be interpreted separately.

The contribution is a combined tracking and gesture recognition system designed for real-time operation on existing hardware. Its results support reliable performance across the people and rooms represented in the test set. The demonstrated gesture vocabulary is specifically the distinction between an open hand and a closed hand.
neurips-1994-a-convolutional-neural-netw.tldr: A convolutional neural network system tracks hands and recognizes open or closed gestures with high reported accuracy across multiple users and rooms.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a network that grows while learning the structure of a collection of input vectors. Its goal is to capture important topological relationships: how different parts of the input data relate to one another. Learning therefore concerns both the units used to represent the data and the connections that express relationships among those units.

The model uses a simple Hebb-like learning rule and can add units and connections as learning proceeds. Unlike the earlier neural gas approach described in the abstract, it does not require parameters that change according to a time schedule. It can continue adapting until a chosen performance criterion has been satisfied, connecting the duration of learning to that criterion.

This combination matters because representation size and connectivity can develop during learning rather than being fixed throughout the process. The abstract identifies vector quantization, clustering, and interpolation as applications. Across these uses, the shared contribution is an incremental representation that learns relationships in the data while expanding its own structure.
neurips-1994-a-growing-neural-gas-networ.tldr: Growing neural gas learns relationships among inputs by adding units and connections until a performance criterion is met.

paragraphs: This paper develops a training method for a feedforward optical network whose processing is distributed continuously across space. The network consists of thin layers of Kerr-type material, where the refractive index depends on local light intensity. Consequently, one light pattern can influence how another beam travels through the material, providing a physical mechanism for nonlinear processing.

The authors derive learning from a Lagrangian formulation of constrained output-error minimization. This mathematical approach accounts for the network's physical constraints while determining how its internal weights should change. The resulting procedure computes a spatial pattern of error at the output and reflects that signal backward through the device to assign errors to internal layers.

Those internal error patterns guide updates to the weighting values. The contribution is therefore a formulation of backpropagation suited to continuous optical signals and nondiscrete neurons. The paper presents computer simulations of training and discusses a simple optical-table demonstration, connecting the mathematical derivation with simulated learning and a physical implementation concept.
neurips-1994-a-lagrangian-formulation-fo.tldr: A constrained optimization formulation derives spatially distributed backpropagation for training a nonlinear optical network.

paragraphs: The paper models how odor molecules interact with receptor proteins and how those proteins activate a second messenger. It treats chemosensory reception as a sequence of chemical reactions whose behavior can be described mathematically. The aim is to connect these reaction mechanisms to experimental measurements of sensory neurons.

The authors transform the reaction-kinetics equations into a feedforward artificial neural network. This makes neural network learning algorithms available for fitting the model's parameters. Crucially, the adjustable weights correspond to chemical parameters, so training changes quantities with a meaning in the underlying reaction model. Experimental observations become examples from which those parameter values can be learned.

The model is demonstrated using data from honey bee chemosensory neurons. The authors report that it can reproduce the observed data, whereas simpler models cannot do so. This supports the adequacy of the proposed reaction model for those observations. The broader methodological contribution is using a neural network representation to fit a mechanistic chemical model directly to experimental evidence.
neurips-1994-a-model-for-chemosensory-re.tldr: A neural network representation of chemical reaction kinetics fits honey bee sensory data that simpler models cannot reproduce.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the cost of searching stored prototypes when classification must tolerate transformations of an input pattern. It builds on tangent-distance methods, retaining their categorization rule while changing how candidate prototypes are searched. The central aim is to reduce the number of tangent-distance calculations needed to reach a classification decision.

The method organizes prototypes in a graph that records transformation constraints and geometric relationships during learning. At classification time, an improved graph search criterion uses that structure to guide the search. This makes the organization of the stored examples an important part of the computational method, because it helps determine which comparisons need to be performed.

The authors state that the method has the same theoretical recognition accuracy as the tangent-distance approaches using the same rule. On a handwriting recognition task, a basic implementation requires less than half the computation of Euclidean sorting. The reported benefit is therefore faster classification through fewer distance evaluations while preserving the underlying decision rule.
neurips-1994-a-rapid-graph-based-method-.tldr: A graph-guided prototype search reduces tangent-distance computations while preserving the underlying transformation-invariant classification rule.

paragraphs: This paper presents a fabricated analog chip implementing a modified ART1 clustering network. The modification makes the architecture more suitable for integrated circuitry while preserving the original algorithm's computational properties. The contribution includes working hardware and experimental chip tests, bringing the clustering procedure into a physical implementation.

A single chip contains 100 input-layer nodes and 18 category-layer nodes, allowing it to cluster patterns of 100 binary pixels into as many as 18 categories. The design also supports expansion through an array of chips without additional interfacing circuitry. Increasing one array dimension enlarges the input layer, while increasing the other expands the category layer.

Although the internal computation is analog, the chip communicates with external equipment using digital signals and behaves asynchronously. That interface allows testing with equipment intended for digital chips. The abstract reports an equivalent processing rate of 2.2 billion connections and connection updates per second. Together, the implementation and expansion scheme show how specialized neural hardware can combine analog computation with digital system integration.
neurips-1994-a-real-time-clustering-cmos.tldr: A fabricated ART1 clustering chip combines analog computation, digital interfaces, and modular expansion for rapid binary-pattern classification.

paragraphs: This paper tackles classification errors caused by deformed input patterns. Its Adaptive Input Field Neural Network combines an already trained neural network with an elastic input field attached to the input layer. The adjustable field gives the system a way to compensate for deformation while keeping the classifier itself fixed.

An iterative procedure determines an optimal affine adjustment of the input field. The method therefore changes how the pattern is presented to the network, making input adaptation part of recognition. The authors also establish convergence of the algorithm, providing a mathematical result about the behavior of the repeated adjustment process.

In handwritten numeral recognition, the system correctly categorizes 10.83% of the patterns that were originally misclassified. That percentage refers to recovered errors, rather than an increase of 10.83 percentage points in overall accuracy. Total recognition performance improves without modifying the pretrained network. The result supports adapting the input representation as a way to recover some deformation-related errors from an existing classifier.
neurips-1994-adaptive-elastic-input-fiel.tldr: An adaptive input field corrects some handwritten numeral errors by compensating for deformation without changing the pretrained classifier.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether learning a new motor behavior can undo the benefits of an earlier learning experience. This is catastrophic interference: the same capacity for change that enables adaptation can also disrupt an existing skill. The authors investigate this issue through human behavioral experiments and computational modeling in a dynamic motor learning task.

Subjects show interference under some conditions but appear protected from it under others. The authors interpret this contrast as evidence that motor learning can consolidate, meaning that a learned behavior can become more resistant to disruption. The finding makes the conditions surrounding successive learning experiences central to understanding whether earlier learning survives.

To explain the behavioral results, the authors use a modular neural network with both rapidly changing and slowly changing connections. Modularity supports learning multiple input-output mappings, while the two connection timescales incorporate different rates of adaptation. This combination accounts for the reported behavioral pattern, linking the possibility of consolidation to a model that accommodates both change and retention.
neurips-1994-catastrophic-interference-i.tldr: Human motor learning shows condition-dependent interference that a modular network with fast and slow connections can explain.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a factorial learning algorithm motivated by segmentation problems in vision. Its underlying factors correspond to groups of strongly correlated input features. This sets up learning as a search for components that can jointly explain an example, allowing multiple factors to contribute to the same observed input.

The key change concerns what cluster generators compete over. In the proposed model, they compete to explain individual features and cooperate to explain whole examples. Traditional clustering, as described in the abstract, organizes this relationship the other way around. By moving competition to the feature level, the method supports an explanation assembled from several feature groups.

An extension recovers hierarchical models when data come from multiple unknown categories, each with its own structure of multiple causes. This adds category organization to the factor-based explanation of individual examples. Several simulations demonstrate the approach. The central contribution is a clustering formulation designed to uncover cooperating factors, together with a hierarchical extension for data whose causal organization differs across categories.
neurips-1994-factorial-learning-by-clust.tldr: A clustering algorithm discovers factors by making generators compete over features and cooperate to explain complete examples.

paragraphs: The paper examines a tempting response to large reinforcement learning problems: replace a table of values with a function approximator that generalizes across inputs. This can address the growth in the number of values that must be represented as a problem becomes larger. Neural networks are one example of such an approximator.

The authors show that combining function approximation with dynamic programming can be unreliable. Even cases described as benign can produce an entirely wrong policy, meaning that the resulting action choices can be wrong. The issue therefore concerns the behavior produced by learning, as well as whether the numerical updates settle down.

The paper introduces Grow-Support as an algorithm that avoids divergence while retaining the possibility of useful generalization. Its contribution is to pair a diagnosis of instability with an approach designed around a stability guarantee. The meaning of safety here is specifically protection from divergence. The abstract positions that property as a way to preserve the benefits of approximation without accepting the instability of the straightforward combination.
neurips-1994-generalization-in-reinforce.tldr: Grow-Support addresses divergence that can arise when dynamic programming uses a generalizing value-function approximator.

paragraphs: This paper studies hyperparameter selection when a learner cannot perfectly represent the rule generating its data. The learner is a linear perceptron, while the teacher can be nonlinear. In the nonlinear setting, the rule is called unrealisable because some error remains unavoidable for that student, regardless of how its parameters are chosen.

Using a statistical mechanical formulation, the authors calculate evidence, generalization error, and a consistency measure. Their model moves between a linear teacher and a nonlinear teacher, allowing them to examine how representational mismatch changes the relationship between these quantities. They compare hyperparameters selected by maximizing evidence with those that directly optimize the performance measures.

For the nonlinear case, evidence maximization can give misleading guidance about performance. The study nevertheless finds circumstances in which it remains useful despite being suboptimal. The result is a qualified assessment of evidence-based selection: its preferred hyperparameters need not produce the best predictions when the student's model class cannot express the teacher's rule.
neurips-1994-hyperparameters-evidence-an.tldr: Evidence maximization can select suboptimal hyperparameters when a linear learner cannot represent a nonlinear teacher.

paragraphs: This paper addresses reinforcement learning with hidden state, where the information currently available to the learner is insufficient to distinguish relevant situations. Its proposed method, instance-based state identification, builds short-term memory during learning. The purpose of that memory is to supply enough recent context to resolve ambiguity about the state.

The approach draws on a similarity between hidden-state learning and learning in continuous geometric spaces. It applies instance-based, or memory-based, learning, a method the abstract identifies as successful in continuous spaces. This choice connects the problem of identifying a hidden situation with a learning approach organized around individual instances.

The authors report learning with an order of magnitude fewer training steps than several previous approaches. The stated benefit combines efficiency with online construction of the memory needed for disambiguation. The contribution is therefore a way to learn a useful state representation as experience arrives, using short-term context to make hidden-state reinforcement learning more tractable.
neurips-1994-instance-based-state-identi.tldr: Instance-based state identification builds short-term memory online to resolve hidden states while reducing reported training requirements.

paragraphs: The paper presents an alternating minimization algorithm for training radial basis function and linear regressor networks. Alternating minimization divides an optimization procedure into two steps that are pursued in turn. The authors focus on how to implement those steps with convergence guarantees, making the behavior of the training procedure the central issue.

Their algorithm modifies a small-step interior point method originally used for primal linear programs. This connects network training to a mathematical optimization method with an analyzed iteration count. The abstract reports a convergence rate expressed in terms of network size and the accuracy of the resulting solution, linking the computational requirement to both problem scale and precision.

Two additional results describe how aggressively the two alternating steps may be pursued while ensuring convergence of each step. These conditions matter because making larger or more ambitious updates must remain compatible with the algorithm's convergence properties. The contribution is an optimization-based training construction supported by explicit analysis of update aggressiveness and convergence.
neurips-1994-interior-point-implementati.tldr: An interior point approach gives alternating network training convergence analysis and conditions on how aggressively its two steps can proceed.

paragraphs: This paper studies query learning when a student cannot perfectly learn its teacher. Instead of receiving random examples, the learner selects queries intended to gain information. The authors examine a linear perceptron student learning a binary perceptron teacher, using this mismatch to investigate whether information-seeking queries actually improve generalization.

They compare two ways to reduce uncertainty. Minimum student space entropy queries target uncertainty in the student's possible models and are appropriate when the teacher's model space is unknown. Minimum teacher space entropy queries target uncertainty about the teacher and assume that its model space is known, even though a simpler student has deliberately been chosen.

For student-space queries, effectiveness depends on the structure of the student's model space. Teacher-space queries produce higher generalization error than random examples in the studied setting because query selection lacks feedback about the student's progress. The finding shows why acquiring information about the teacher can be poorly aligned with improving a learner whose representational capacity is more limited.
neurips-1994-learning-from-queries-for-m.tldr: Queries that maximize information about a teacher can hurt a simpler student's generalization when selection ignores the student's progress.

paragraphs: The paper gives a statistical learning method for stochastic perceptrons. These models produce an output of one with a probability determined by applying an activation function to a weighted input sum minus a threshold. The learning result permits arbitrary monotonic activation functions, while restricting each weight to minus one, zero, or plus one.

The guarantee applies when input examples come from a family called k-blocking distributions. This extends the analysis beyond statistically independent input variables. In particular, the abstract states that the 2k-blocking family includes all Markov distributions of order k, so the supported distributions accommodate specified forms of dependence between inputs.

The method PAC learns the stated model class, providing a formal learnability result under these assumptions. The same algorithm accommodates both nondecreasing and nonincreasing activation functions on the Boolean domain, including the sigmoid and usual radial basis cases identified by the authors. Its contribution is a common learning procedure that combines activation-function flexibility with a distribution family broader than independent inputs.
neurips-1994-learning-stochastic-percept.tldr: A statistical algorithm PAC learns restricted-weight stochastic perceptrons with monotonic activations under a family of dependent input distributions.

paragraphs: The paper presents NeuroChess, a program that learns from the final outcomes of chess games. Its learned component is a board evaluation function represented by an artificial neural network. Such a function assigns an assessment to a board position, making position evaluation the concrete target of the learning process.

NeuroChess combines inductive neural network learning, temporal differencing, and a variant of explanation-based learning. These ingredients bring together learning from examples, learning across successive positions, and an explanation-based component. Their integration addresses the challenge posed by the training signal: the final outcome belongs to an entire game, while the evaluation function must assess positions encountered within it.

The paper reports performance results illustrating both strengths and weaknesses of this approach. The stated contribution is a working combination of learning methods for acquiring chess evaluations from game outcomes. It frames chess learning around improving the judgment of board positions and examines what that combination can achieve through the program's observed performance.
neurips-1994-learning-to-play-the-game-o.tldr: NeuroChess learns neural board evaluations from game outcomes by combining temporal differencing, inductive learning, and explanation-based learning.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how the macaque lateral geniculate nucleus develops its layered organization. The observed layering pattern changes midway through the nucleus, near small gaps associated with the retina's blind spot. The authors ask whether these localized gaps can help explain a change in the structure of the larger tissue.

They construct a three-dimensional developmental model driven by local interactions between cells. These interactions produce a wave of receptive-field development that travels through the nucleus and establishes two distinct layering patterns. The model therefore connects local developmental behavior to the formation of an organized structure across the nucleus.

By examining how the developmental wave interacts with the gaps, the authors find that the gaps induce the change in layering pattern in the model. This supplies a mechanism linking a localized irregularity to a broader anatomical transition. The study also explores factors that determine general organization, with the central result showing how development can amplify the structural influence of a small spatial disruption.
neurips-1994-morphogenesis-of-the-latera.tldr: A three-dimensional developmental model shows how blind-spot-related gaps can redirect the larger layering pattern of the lateral geniculate nucleus.

paragraphs: The paper addresses two linked questions in matching point sets: which points correspond, and how the sets are positioned relative to one another. These questions arise together because the apparent match between points depends on alignment. The authors propose an algorithm that handles noisy sets, unequal numbers of points, and differences that can include nonrigid transformations.

Two variants cover different alignment models. The two-dimensional version estimates an affine transformation, including translation, rotation, scale, and shear. The three-dimensional version estimates translation and rotation between two three-dimensional point sets. These distinctions specify the transformations recovered by each version of the method.

The authors derive an objective from mean field theory and minimize it using clocked dynamics resembling expectation-maximization. This provides a shared optimization formulation for pose and correspondence. Experiments on handwritten and synthetic data offer empirical support for the approach. The contribution is a robust, readily implementable matching procedure designed to cope with point sets that do not arrive as clean, equally sized copies.
neurips-1994-new-algorithms-for-2d-and-3.tldr: A mean-field-based optimization method jointly estimates point correspondences and alignment for noisy two- and three-dimensional data.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to interpolate between specified images in a sequence. The task is to construct intermediate images that connect the available observations. It matters for model-based vision because the images provide samples of a changing visual process, and interpolation supplies a way to represent what happens between those samples.

The authors approach the problem through manifold learning. This frames interpolation in terms of learning the structure of the image sequence, giving the method a basis for nonlinear relationships between images. The title and abstract place this learned structure at the center of how intermediate images are obtained.

The work arose during development of a system combining lip-reading with speech recognition, providing a concrete motivation for handling image sequences. Results are presented on both synthetic and real sequences. The contribution is the application of manifold learning to nonlinear image interpolation, supported by demonstrations on those two kinds of data and motivated by visual information in a speech-related system.
neurips-1994-nonlinear-image-interpolati.tldr: The paper applies manifold learning to nonlinear interpolation between images, motivated by a combined lip-reading and speech recognition system.

paragraphs: The paper investigates what networks of spiking neurons can compute and how much training data they require. Its starting point is that the timing of neural events can participate in information processing. The authors introduce a formal network model intended to capture important timing phenomena, including synaptic modulation, so these questions can be studied mathematically.

A central distinction is between unlimited and limited timing precision. Unlimited precision allows arbitrarily fine distinctions in event times, whereas limited precision restricts those distinctions. Analyzing both cases makes the timing assumption explicit when assessing computational power, rather than treating precision as an unspecified property of the model.

The authors prove upper and lower bounds on computational power and on the number of examples needed for training. These results address both capability and learning complexity within the formal framework. The contribution is an analytical account of spiking computation that places mathematical bounds on what timing-based networks can achieve and what their learning requirements can be.
neurips-1994-on-the-computational-comple.tldr: A formal spiking-network model yields bounds on computational power and training-example requirements under different timing-precision assumptions.

paragraphs: The paper introduces an image compression method built around a neural network structure called a PCA pyramid. Its first step is to show how neural networks can operate within a pyramidal framework. This makes a hierarchy of representations the organizing structure for the compression method, connecting neural learning with pyramid-based image processing.

The resulting compression approach is described as similar to the Laplace pyramid and wavelet transform. Those comparisons locate its contribution in a family of structured image representations, with the PCA pyramid supplying the learned component. The authors report experiments on real images, applying the representation to the image compression task that motivates the work.

The paper also presents a way to combine quantization with learning the pyramid. Quantization concerns the discrete values used to encode a representation, so incorporating it into learning connects representation formation with the encoding stage. The overall contribution brings together the neural pyramid, its use for compression, and a method for learning it alongside quantization.
neurips-1994-pca-pyramids-for-image-comp.tldr: PCA pyramids combine neural network image representations with a compression method that can learn alongside quantization.

paragraphs: This paper studies the curvature of cost functions used to train recurrent neural networks. It analyzes a layered, fully recurrent architecture that includes conventional feedforward networks as a special case. This provides a framework for examining how recurrent connections affect the optimization problem while retaining a connection to feedforward architectures.

The authors describe a recursive computation of the full Hessian, the matrix that records second-order changes in the cost function with respect to weights. They also discuss simplifying approximations. Their analysis shows how weight decay can smooth the cost function and substantially assist training, linking a regularization mechanism to the geometry of optimization.

The paper then presents tentative pruning results using Optimal Brain Surgeon. These results demonstrate that recurrent networks can construct an efficient internal memory. The contribution combines mathematical machinery for studying recurrent-network curvature with an initial application to removing weights, connecting the organization of a network's parameters to the compactness of the memory it develops.
neurips-1994-recurrent-networks-second-o.tldr: The paper analyzes recurrent-network cost curvature, explains how weight decay assists training, and presents tentative pruning results for efficient internal memory.

paragraphs: Young barn owls raised with optical prisms shift their auditory spatial maps to align with altered visual information. The puzzling detail is where this adaptation occurs. The first convergence of visual and auditory information is in the optic tectum, but the relevant plasticity occurs earlier, in the inferior colliculus.

The authors model this remapping with a global reinforcement signal controlled by visual foveation. A Hebbian learning rule, gated by that signal, adjusts the auditory maps appropriately. Although weights are permitted to change throughout the auditory system, the learning procedure preferentially changes weights in the inferior colliculus, matching the location observed in the owl.

This result offers an explanation for how a learning signal can produce anatomically selective adaptation without restricting all change to a predetermined site. The authors suggest that the location of learning could emerge from the interaction between the learning procedure and network architecture. Their model supports that possibility by reproducing both map adjustment and its preferred anatomical location.
neurips-1994-reinforcement-learning-pred.tldr: A reinforcement-gated learning model reproduces auditory remapping and preferentially changes the same brain region implicated in barn owls.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes how generalization changes during training for a general nonlinear learning machine. It considers training on a random sample using gradient descent to reduce training error. The question is about the course of learning: how performance beyond the training sample evolves while optimization continues to improve the training objective.

The main result is that the best generalization generally occurs before the global minimum of training error is reached. This establishes a distinction between the point favored by continued training-error reduction and the point with the best generalization. It gives a rigorous basis for treating training duration as relevant to predictive performance.

The analysis also separates the complexity of the whole machine class from the complexity of the particular machine being learned. Those are different quantities: one concerns the available family of models, and the other concerns an individual member during learning. The contribution clarifies their distinct roles while explaining why progress on the training objective need not track progress in generalization.
neurips-1994-temporal-dynamics-of-genera.tldr: A theoretical analysis shows that generalization generally peaks before training error reaches its global minimum.

paragraphs: The paper proposes an unsupervised approach to categorizing three-dimensional objects from their two-dimensional projected views. Its starting point is an auto-associative network that encodes views of a single object into a representation indicating viewing direction. This connects the changing appearance of an object to a representation of how it is being viewed.

The authors build two classification models around this capability. The first selects the auto-associative network whose reconstructed view most closely matches the input. The second uses a modular architecture with an additional network that classifies views by dividing the input space nonlinearly. The two models therefore make category decisions through different mechanisms.

Simulations using three-dimensional wire-frame objects demonstrate the effectiveness of both proposed models. The contribution is a way to use learned view representations for object categorization, with reconstruction matching and nonlinear classification as alternative decision methods. The stated demonstration concerns projected views of wire-frame objects, grounding the results in that particular visual setting.
neurips-1994-unsupervised-classification.tldr: Two unsupervised models categorize projected views of 3D objects using auto-associative representations that encode viewing direction.
